section_summary: This section consists chiefly of public appeals asking President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Secretary of State Cordell Hull to halt American exports of arms, scrap iron, trucks, oil, and other war materials to Japan during its war in China. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act of 1937 could embargo only specified arms and only after a presidential proclamation recognizing a state of war, while raw materials such as scrap iron were outside executive authority. The section also contains missionary accounts of Japanese bombing in China, antiwar articles and resolutions, and extensive petitions from Vermont and the San Diego area.

keywords: Office of Arms and Munitions Control

subfiles.title: Letter from Max H. Webster protesting American trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Webster protests American participation in Japan's attack on China through sales of munitions and essential war materials.
subfiles.summary: Webster calls the government's posture of neutrality hypocritical while American commerce supplies Japan's war effort. He argues that present profits will produce future armament costs and undermine the United States' claim to be a good neighbor.

subfiles.title: Reply to Max H. Webster concerning the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The Department explains why it lacks authority to stop exports to Japan without a presidential neutrality proclamation.
subfiles.summary: Green states that a proclamation recognizing war between China and Japan would embargo arms to both belligerents, not Japan alone. The Neutrality Act does not permit restrictions on commodities outside the statutory arms list. He supplies export-license totals of about $14.27 million for China and $10.79 million for Japan since July 1, 1937.

subfiles.title: Letter from Mary Stewart urging an end to war supplies and loans to Japan
subfiles.about: Stewart asks Hull to stop munitions, war materials, and loans from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Stewart condemns Japan's warfare and mistreatment of Chinese civilians. Citing America's alleged provision of 54.4 percent of Japanese war materials, she argues that the United States is implicated in the aggression and that Japan will grow increasingly dependent on American supplies.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mary Stewart concerning exports and loans to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department outlines the statutory limits on embargoing Japan and addresses Stewart's concern about loans.
subfiles.summary: The reply repeats that invoking the Neutrality Act would stop arms exports to China as well as Japan and would not cover non-arms commodities. It provides the Department's arms-license figures for both belligerents. Green adds that the government has sanctioned no loans to Japan and knows of no Japanese borrowing in the United States.

subfiles.title: Letter from Ralph H. Read to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Read asks Roosevelt to end the war-sustaining trade between the United States and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The minister argues that American commerce has made the United States a partner in Japan's Far Eastern conflict. He emphasizes the destruction of Chinese lives and property among a people with whom Americans had long maintained friendly relations.

subfiles.title: Reply to Ralph H. Read
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds to Read's request by explaining the Neutrality Act and providing arms-export figures.
subfiles.summary: Yost says that without a presidential proclamation there is no statutory basis for stopping arms exports. Such a proclamation would embargo China and Japan alike, while the act cannot reach commodities outside the arms list. He cites licensed exports of roughly $14.27 million to China and $10.79 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter from B. N. Hamilton advocating noncooperation with Japanese aggression
subfiles.about: Hamilton urges a boycott of munitions, oil, scrap iron, and other war materials destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton contrasts official protests over the closing of the Open Door in China with continued American sales that enable Japanese aggression. He asks whether the United States can quarantine Japan and adopt a policy of noncooperation with aggressors. A material boycott, he argues, would be more effective than verbal protests.

subfiles.title: Reply to B. N. Hamilton
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department gives its standard legal explanation for not imposing an embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that the Neutrality Act requires a presidential finding of war before arms exports can be stopped and that any resulting embargo would apply to China too. He notes that the act covers only enumerated arms, ammunition, and implements of war. Export-license totals for China and Japan are again supplied.

subfiles.title: Letter from Eva M. Brallier transmitting an article on trade with dictatorships
subfiles.about: Brallier sends an article advocating democratic economic action against aggressor states.
subfiles.summary: Brallier says she is deeply interested in American trade with Japan. She reports placing related material with the Daily Mail and Populaire in Paris and encloses an article for Hull's consideration.

subfiles.title: Article advocating a democratic trade embargo against aggressor nations
subfiles.about: The article proposes coordinated democratic economic pressure as an alternative to war and appeasement.
subfiles.summary: Brallier argues that fear following the Munich Pact has driven democracies toward rearmament while dictatorships conquer weaker peoples. She condemns Mussolini's conquest of Ethiopia, Hitler's expansion, and Japan's devastation of China, especially the bombing of civilians. A united embargo—particularly ending purchases of Japanese silk and sales of scrap iron—is presented as a lesser sacrifice than another war.

subfiles.title: Reply to Eva M. Brallier
subfiles.about: Green explains that existing law does not permit an executive embargo on scrap iron and describes the government's position on civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Green thanks Brallier for her article but says scrap iron is deliberately excluded from the Neutrality Act's definition of arms. He repeats that invoking the act would embargo arms to both China and Japan. The letter also states that the government has publicly condemned bombing civilians and has communicated that position to American aircraft manufacturers and exporters.

subfiles.title: Ladies Missionary Society petition against assistance to Japan
subfiles.from: Alice C. Greene and other members of the Ladies Missionary Society
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: The petition asks the federal government to prevent American resources from aiding Japan's aggression against China.
subfiles.summary: The petition declares that American suppliers furnish a substantial share of the materials enabling Japanese outrages in China. Its signatories call on the President and Congress to prevent government or private resources from aiding Japan either directly or indirectly. Most of the document consists of several pages of signatures.

subfiles.title: Reply to Alice C. Greene and the Ladies Missionary Society
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the society's petition and explains the limits of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Greene and the other petitioners and encloses the Neutrality Act and International Traffic in Arms. He explains that a proclamation would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan but that other commodities cannot be embargoed under the act. The familiar licensed-export totals are included.

subfiles.title: Letter from Milton Ernest Fish concerning aid to Japan's war machine
subfiles.about: Fish asks what can be done immediately to stop Americans from supplying Japan's mechanized war.
subfiles.summary: Fish praises Hull's Nashville denunciation of naked force and describes his contacts with Chinese communities and missionaries. He argues that official criticism of Japan appears hypocritical while American profiteers supply essential materials. He asks for immediate action before more Chinese noncombatants are killed.

subfiles.title: Reply to Milton Ernest Fish
subfiles.about: Yost responds to Fish with the Department's legal explanation and its condemnation of civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Yost appreciates Fish's comments about Hull's Nashville address and reviews the Neutrality Act's proclamation mechanism. He notes that an embargo would apply to China and Japan alike and only to enumerated military articles. The letter supplies export-license figures and says aircraft firms have been told of the government's opposition to bombing civilians.

subfiles.title: Letter from Albert H. Flagge forwarding a missionary's account
subfiles.about: Flagge forwards Gladys Stephenson's letter as evidence supporting his church's petition to stop arms shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Flagge says the enclosed missionary letter contains a marked passage that inspired his congregation's appeal. He asks the President to do everything possible to end shipments of arms to Japan.

subfiles.title: Gladys Stephenson's letter from Hankow describing air raids
subfiles.about: Stephenson recounts Japanese bombing, civilian casualties, medical work, and missionary endurance in Hankow and Wuchang.
subfiles.summary: Stephenson describes devastating air raids that struck a maternity hospital, refugee shelter, boats, and neighborhoods near the Methodist hospital. She recounts triage, amputations, traumatized children, refugee journeys, and the decision of missionaries to remain despite the expected invasion of Hankow. She is distressed to find American and British markings on bomb fragments and closes with stories of Christian courage and verses by John Oxenham.

subfiles.title: Reply to Albert H. Flagge
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Stephenson's letter and explains the statutory position on arms exports.
subfiles.summary: Yost notes that the Department had already received another copy of Stephenson's account. He explains that recognizing a state of war would stop arms shipments to both belligerents and that the Neutrality Act cannot regulate other commodities. Updated figures cite approximately $14.22 million in licensed arms exports to China and $10.79 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter from Mrs. R. A. Panzer challenging Roosevelt's Far Eastern policy
subfiles.about: Panzer asks why Roosevelt has not recognized the Sino-Japanese war and applied the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Panzer argues that the war has been an obvious fact for nearly a year and a half and questions whether China's losses, including Canton, still justify the policy. She links continued assistance to Japan with increased American spending on Pacific fortifications. She also asks Roosevelt to clarify his Chicago call for quarantining aggressor nations.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. R. A. Panzer
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department defends Roosevelt's discretionary decision not to invoke the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that without a proclamation there is no legal authority to prohibit arms exports to Japan alone or to both belligerents. He emphasizes that non-arms commodities fall outside the act. The President, he says, concluded that invoking the resolution would not serve the broad interests of the United States and its people.

subfiles.title: Carl E. Mapes's transmittal of Doris Dunham's protest
subfiles.about: Mapes forwards a constituent's protest against exports of scrap iron and trucks to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The congressman encloses Doris Dunham's letter and asks Hull for a response that Mapes can transmit to her.

subfiles.title: Letter from Doris Dunham on scrap iron and truck exports
subfiles.about: Dunham asks whether Congress can prohibit American scrap iron and trucks from being sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dunham argues that the materials will be used to subjugate China even as the United States expands its own armaments out of fear of Japan. She also warns that a victorious Japan could use Chinese labor and resources to undercut American goods in world markets.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Carl E. Mapes
subfiles.about: The Department suggests a response explaining that only Congress can enact restrictions on scrap iron and trucks.
subfiles.summary: The letter proposes that Mapes send Dunham copies of the Neutrality Act and International Traffic in Arms. It explains that the executive can prohibit only enumerated arms after a war proclamation and that no existing statute authorizes a ban on scrap iron or trucks. New legislation is identified as a matter for Congress.

subfiles.title: Letter from Kate H. Dewing challenging official arms-export comparisons
subfiles.from: Kate H. Dewing, San Diego Peace Committee and Women's International League for Peace and Freedom
subfiles.to: Department of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Dewing submits additional petitions and argues that licensed-arms figures obscure the much larger American contribution of scrap iron and other strategic materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dewing replies to an earlier departmental letter concerning 983 signatures and disputes its comparison of licensed arms exports to China and Japan. She cites more than $35 million in American scrap-iron sales to Japan in 1937 and argues that the United States supplies nearly half of Japan's essential war imports. She presents moral, strategic, economic, and democratic grounds for an embargo and encloses 1,076 signatures and a ministerial resolution.

subfiles.title: Newspaper clipping on economic penalties against Germany and San Diego scrap exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Lee G. Miller and Harold Keen
subfiles.about: The clipping combines an article on presidential tariff powers against Nazi Germany with a report on 5,000 tons of San Diego scrap iron awaiting shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Miller explains how Section 338 of the Hawley-Smoot Tariff Act might permit Roosevelt to penalize German discrimination against American commerce, with discussion of helium restrictions and Matthew Woll's criticism of Treasury policy. Keen reports that the freighter Spyros is expected to take 5,000 tons of scrap metal from Pier 1 to Japanese mills. The latter article contrasts profits for junk dealers with protests by San Diego peace and church groups.

subfiles.title: San Diego County Ministerial Association resolution
subfiles.about: The association unanimously protests shipments of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The certified resolution records unanimous action at the association's regular meeting of November 7, 1938. Secretary Harold E. Walker attests to the decision.

subfiles.title: San Diego petitions protesting war-material shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Residents of San Diego and nearby California communities
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: The signatories protest shipments of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: These standardized petition sheets ask Roosevelt and Hull to stop American scrap iron and other war supplies from reaching Japan. They contain hundreds of signatures and addresses from San Diego, National City, Long Beach, La Jolla, Ramona, and other California communities. The sheets form part of the larger submission described by Kate H. Dewing.
